claim: For M. tuberculosis to cause disease, the bacillus must export effector proteins to the host-pathogen interface.
source: For M. tuberculosis to cause disease, the bacillus must export effector proteins to the host-pathogen interface.

claim: Effector proteins enable M. tuberculosis to grow in macrophages and avoid clearance by the host immune response.

source: SecA2 is a paralog of the SecA ATPase of the general Sec protein export pathway.

claim: The general Sec pathway transports preproteins with N-terminal signal sequences across the inner membrane through a channel comprised of SecY, SecE and SecG proteins.

claim: Preproteins must be in an unfolded state to travel through the SecYEG channel.
source: Preproteins must be in an unfolded state to travel through the SecYEG channel and, in Gram-negative bacteria, the SecB chaperone binds a subset of preproteins to maintain them in an unfolded translocation competent state.

claim: In Gram-negative bacteria, the SecB chaperone binds a subset of preproteins to maintain them in an unfolded translocation competent state.
source: Preproteins must be in an unfolded state to travel through the SecYEG channel and, in Gram-negative bacteria, the SecB chaperone binds a subset of preproteins to maintain them in an unfolded translocation competent state.

claim: Following export across the membrane, the signal sequence is cleaved and the mature protein is released.

evidence: Supported by citation to Tsirigotaki et al., 2017

claim: All bacteria possess an essential Sec pathway that carries out the majority of protein export.
source: While all bacteria possess an essential Sec pathway that carries out the majority of protein export, only mycobacteria and a subset of Gram-positive bacteria possess specialized Sec export systems that are defined by a second SecA (Bensing et al., 2014; Miller et al., 2017).

claim: Only mycobacteria and a subset of Gram-positive bacteria possess specialized Sec export systems that are defined by a second SecA.
source: While all bacteria possess an essential Sec pathway that carries out the majority of protein export, only mycobacteria and a subset of Gram-positive bacteria possess specialized Sec export systems that are defined by a second SecA (Bensing et al., 2014; Miller et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bensing et al., 2014 and Miller et al., 2017

claim: In organisms with SecA2, SecA1 is the name given to the canonical SecA and the specialized SecA is named SecA2.

claim: For the mycobacterial SecA2 system, the housekeeping SecYEG channel, and possibly SecA1, are also involved.

claim: SecA1 and SecA2 are functionally distinct, as shown by their inability to compensate for the loss of one another.
source: However, SecA1 and SecA2 are functionally distinct, as shown by their inability to compensate for the loss of one another (Braunstein et al., 2001; Rigel et al., 2009), and it remains unclear how SecA2 functions to export its relatively small and specific subset of proteins.

claim: It remains unclear how SecA2 functions to export its relatively small and specific subset of proteins.

claim: A suppressor screen was carried out using a dominant negative secA2 K129R mutant of Mycobacterium smegmatis to identify new components of the mycobacterial SecA2 pathway.
source: Here, we carried out a suppressor screen using a dominant negative secA2 K129R mutant of Mycobacterium smegmatis, a fast-growing model mycobacteria, as a means to identify new components of the mycobacterial SecA2 pathway.
evidence: Description of experimental approach used in this study

claim: The K129R substitution is in the ATP binding site of SecA2.
source: The K129R substitution is in the ATP binding site of SecA2, and past studies lead to a model where SecA2 K129R is defective for SecA2-dependent export but still able to interact with its normal binding partners that include SecYEG (Rigel et al., 2009; Ligon et al., 2013).

claim: SecA2 K129R is defective for SecA2-dependent export but still able to interact with its normal binding partners that include SecYEG.
source: The K129R substitution is in the ATP binding site of SecA2, and past studies lead to a model where SecA2 K129R is defective for SecA2-dependent export but still able to interact with its normal binding partners that include SecYEG (Rigel et al., 2009; Ligon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rigel et al., 2009 and Ligon et al., 2013

claim: SecA2 K129R disrupts SecYEG channels at the membrane, which hinders both general Sec and specialized SecA2 export.
source: As a result, SecA2 K129R disrupts SecYEG channels at the membrane, which hinders both general Sec and specialized SecA2 export as evidenced by more severe phenotypes of secA2 K129R than a ΔsecA2 null mutation (Ligon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ligon et al., 2013

claim: secA2 K129R exhibits more severe phenotypes than a ΔsecA2 null mutation.
source: As a result, SecA2 K129R disrupts SecYEG channels at the membrane, which hinders both general Sec and specialized SecA2 export as evidenced by more severe phenotypes of secA2 K129R than a ΔsecA2 null mutation (Ligon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ligon et al., 2013

claim: A large collection of secA2 K129R suppressor mutations mapped to msmeg_1684, a gene of unknown function renamed satS.
source: A large collection of secA2 K129R suppressor mutations mapped to msmeg_1684, a gene of unknown function that we renamed satS for SecA2 (two) Suppressor.

claim: SatS is present in M. tuberculosis.
source: SatS is also present in M. tuberculosis and, remarkably, the M. tuberculosis satS gene is in an operon with the gene encoding SapM, which is a secreted phosphatase exported by the SecA2 pathway (Zulauf et al., 2018).

claim: The M. tuberculosis satS gene is in an operon with the gene encoding SapM.
source: SatS is also present in M. tuberculosis and, remarkably, the M. tuberculosis satS gene is in an operon with the gene encoding SapM, which is a secreted phosphatase exported by the SecA2 pathway (Zulauf et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zulauf et al., 2018

claim: SapM is a secreted phosphatase exported by the SecA2 pathway.

evidence: Supported by citation to Zulauf et al., 2018

claim: SatS is required for M. tuberculosis growth in macrophages.

claim: SatS functions in the export of SapM and an additional subset of the proteins exported by the SecA2 pathway.
source: Here, we demonstrated that SatS, which we revealed is required for M. tuberculosis growth in macrophages, functions in the export of SapM and an additional subset of the proteins exported by the SecA2 pathway.

claim: SatS exhibits multiple properties of a chaperone, including the ability to bind to and protect substrates from aggregation.
source: We further identify a role for SatS as a protein export chaperone. SatS exhibits multiple properties of a chaperone, including the ability to bind to and protect substrates from aggregation.

claim: The structure of SatS reveals a distinct combination of a new fold and hydrophobic grooves resembling preprotein-binding sites of the SecB chaperone.

claim: Spontaneous suppressor mutants that restored growth on Mueller-Hinton agar were collected from secA2 K129R cultures.
source: Starting with cultures of ∆secA2 expressing the secA2 K129R allele on an integrating plasmid (this strain is referred to as secA2 K129R from hereon), we collected spontaneous suppressor mutants that restored growth on Mueller-Hinton agar.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing of six extragenic suppressors revealed mutations in the same gene msmeg_1684.

claim: Three additional suppressors with mutations in msmeg_1684 were identified by directly sequencing the msmeg_1684 gene and upstream sequence.
source: Three additional suppressors with mutations in msmeg_1684 were identified by directly sequencing the msmeg_1684 gene and upstream sequence in our pool of suppressors (Figure 1B).

claim: Msmeg_1684 is a highly acidic protein with pI 3.83.
source: Msmeg_1684 is a highly acidic protein (pI 3.83) of unknown function with conserved homologs in all mycobacterial species, as well as other actinomycetes (Marmiesse et al., 2004).

claim: Msmeg_1684 has conserved homologs in all mycobacterial species, as well as other actinomycetes.

source: The ∆satS mutant had no in vitro growth defect compared to wild-type M. smegmatis mc2155 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Deletion of satS suppressed the exacerbated phenotypes of secA2 K129R.

claim: The suppression phenotype of ΔsatS could be complemented by adding back a copy of satS from M. smegmatis.
source: Deletion of satS suppressed the exacerbated phenotypes of secA2 K129R, and the suppression phenotype of ΔsatS could be complemented by adding back a copy of satS from M. smegmatis (Figure 1C).

source: Complementation was also successful with the M. tuberculosis satS homolog rv3311 indicating that SatS function is conserved in M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis (Figure 1C).

claim: Wild-type SecA2 is predominantly in the cytoplasm.

claim: The majority of SecA2 K129R is localized to the membrane-containing cell envelope fraction.
source: Unlike wild-type SecA2, which is predominantly in the cytoplasm, the majority of SecA2 K129R is localized to the membrane-containing cell envelope fraction, consistent with SecA2 K129R being trapped in a non-functional complex with SecYEG (Rigel et al., 2009).

claim: Total SecA2 K129R levels were unchanged in the ∆satS background.
source: Total SecA2 K129R levels were unchanged in the ∆satS background (Figure 1D).

claim: SecA2 K129R is associated with reduced levels of SecY.

claim: SatS has a role in the SecA2 export pathway.

source: In M. tuberculosis, the gene encoding SatS is immediately downstream of the gene encoding SapM.

claim: 26 mycobacterial species have conserved sapM-satS gene arrangement.

claim: The ∆satS mutant of M. tuberculosis did not exhibit an in vitro growth defect.
source: The ∆satS mutant of M. tuberculosis did not exhibit an in vitro growth defect (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: A SapM secretion defect was observed in the ∆secA2 mutant.
source: As expected, a SapM secretion defect was observed in the ∆secA2 mutant.

claim: The SapM secretion defect of the ∆satS mutant was reproducibly more severe than the ∆secA2 mutant.
source: Even more striking was the SapM secretion defect of the ∆satS mutant, which was reproducibly more severe than the ∆secA2 mutant (Figure 2A).

claim: There was significantly less phosphatase activity in the supernatant of a ∆secA2 mutant compared to H37Rv.

claim: The ∆satS mutant exhibited an even more severe reduction in secreted phosphatase activity than the ∆secA2 mutant.
source: Consistent with the immunoblot data, there was significantly less phosphatase activity in the supernatant of a ∆secA2 mutant compared to H37Rv, the ∆satS mutant exhibited an even more severe reduction in secreted phosphatase activity, and the ∆satS mutant phenotype could be complemented (Figure 2B).

claim: When M. tuberculosis sapM was expressed in M. smegmatis, SapM was secreted in a SecA2 and SatS dependent manner.

claim: The SapM secretion defect of a ∆satS mutant was more severe than that of a ∆secA2 mutant in M. smegmatis.
source: Again, the SapM secretion defect of a ∆satS mutant was more severe than that of a ∆secA2 mutant and this phenotype could be complemented (Figure 2C).

claim: SatS function is conserved in M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis.

claim: M. smegmatis is a valid model for studying SatS function.

claim: A whole cell assay for measuring secreted SapM phosphatase activity from M. smegmatis grown in 96 well plates was established.

claim: The reduced activity of the ∆satS mutant could be complemented with either SatSMtb or SatSMsm.

claim: The reduction in SapM levels observed in the ∆satS mutant differed from a modest intracellular reduction of SapM in the ∆secA2 mutant.

claim: The reduction in SapM levels in the ∆satS mutant was specific to SapM as the levels of SigA were comparable across strains.

claim: The effect of SatS on SapM levels in the cytoplasm was post-translational.

We favor this role for SatS as it would not only help explain why phenotypes of secA2 K129R depend on the presence of SatS but it is also consistent with our identification of an interaction between SatS and SapM and the chaperone activities of SatS.

source: Although there is a notable lack of amino acid and structural similarity between different types of protein export chaperones, commonalities exist. Protein export chaperones are all highly acidic (pI <5.0) proteins that transiently interact with their substrates in the cytoplasm and remain in the cytoplasm when the substrate is exported (Randall and Hardy, 2002; Thomas et al., 2012; Ekiert and Cox, 2014).
